description: We are a academic team from Brazil, that seek to expand the computational knowledge trough the UFRJ and the EQ (Escola de Química), the institute responsible for engineerings involved in the chemistry and biological areas
summary:
We developed a game with mechanics based off "Reigns", where the player has to choose between two options in each situation that appears for their design plans and the mission itself. The choices made will impact directly on their resources management tab and the final result at the ponctuations table. The game, which we called "for_astronaut", covers each aspect of the process for planning a space mission, from the decisions about duration, objective and communications used and ending at the spaceship creation. Thus, the mission doesn't end there, after all the preparations the game then determines if the choices picked are compatible with the real physics and strategic concepts. 
Realism behind the visuals were one of our focus points, so were the feedbacks and descriptions, that way the player can learn in real time not only the steps to reach the goal, but so how much impact they have in each decision alone.
 As a team, we thought that our main attack proposition to the challenge was to show in a simple format calculations and concepts of the spatial field for students, that can play and learn with each run of the game. It is a quick but insightfull experience that we believe that could help reaching those initial barriers the aspiring space scientists implements around being afraid of not having the required knowledge to understand, visualize and design a mission. 
In conclusion, we've made for_astronauts for the next astronauts.
details:
Game's idea and coding:

Our game started from an idea some of our members had: a spacecraft-building simulator driven by choices. We compared it with games we know from pop culture and designed the choices as A/B decisions, like in “Reigns”. The game is built on that model, in five phases:

1. Mission briefing
The player picks the mission’s science objective (for example, observing the Earth, studying the Moon or flying a space telescope) and the difficulty. Difficulty sets the budget, the mass limit and the deadline.

2. Spacecraft assembly
The player chooses the subsystems: structure, power (panels and batteries), attitude control, computer, communications and science instruments. Each part has a cost, a mass, a power consumption and a science value. Bars at the top of the screen always show the budget, mass and power.

3. Orbit and launcher
The player picks an orbit (low Earth, geostationary, polar or lunar). Each option comes with a short explanation and a simple orbit animation. Launchers have different capacities, and the game warns the player if the rocket is not compatible with the spacecraft’s mass or with the chosen orbit.

4. Mission simulation
The mission runs in stages: launch, transfer and science operations. Random events force decisions, again in the “Reigns” style: a panel failure, a short communication window, low power. The player manages energy, data and propellant. Our original focus was a single-player game, with multiplayer as a possible addition later. As the project grew, we added many more things that can happen during the mission, such as gravitational objects (black holes, wormholes) and other surprises for the pilot, along with actions the player can take to deal with them.

5. Results and scoring
The final grade combines science value, cost efficiency, safety margin and creativity. The game also gives feedback on what worked, what did not, and why.

We also tried to build a mobile version, but we ran out of time. Every update to one version had to be repeated in the other, keeping the same look and the same model

How the code works

The game is written in Python with Pygame. Every decision is a “card” with two choices, and each choice is a set of effects (cost, mass, power use, reliability, schedule, science value). Those effects update a single game-state object, which feeds the bars at the top of the screen. Each phase is a deck of cards. Some cards depend on earlier choices, so a decision in assembly changes which cards appear later. The physics sits in small functions: the rocket equation decides what a launcher can lift, the orbit equations give speed and period, and simple energy and data models track the battery and the downlink. During the flight, random events roll a probability for each risky choice, so a safe plan can still have bad luck. At the end, one function turns the final state into the four scores and the written feedback.

Use of AI

One of our developers used AI tools to write code faster, mainly to save time. He was coding on his phone, so AI made the work easier. He always filtered what it produced and rewrote it whenever necessary. We also used AI to help translate and polish this text, which was written by the team members.

Design and UII:

For_code's marketing members already works in Figma, an online editor, where the league posts and visual identity are designed. One of the marketing members of the league joined our team, and was responsible for the game design, using these existing tools and arts to build the game identity: the league’s color palette and the Lexend font, that are already used in our arts and posts, entirely developed by our members. Everything was designed in 1280x720, the standard resolution, and the elements follow multiples of 36 and 72 so the layouts stay harmonious, similar to what the league already does in its materials.

The astronaut was entirely idealized and drawed by our design member, and was made in Piskel, including its animations and the small background stars. The creative side of the project, and all the original designs, were 100% human-made. AI helped us find the "PiskelApp", a tool not previously used by the league, to turn the idea into pixel art that could go into the game.

AI (Claude) was used in a supporting role. The complete game code was sent, so as the finished designs, together with the league’s visual identity, and it explained the game as a short story, which became the copy for the landing page. It then helped to adapt the previous screens into a landing page that follows the original game design, that will also be reused in the explanatory slides for the game.

Us, 'for_austronat' developers, see this as an alliance between human creativity, which we believe deserves to be valued and credited, and the speed and time savings that AI tools bring to the work. The ideas and the design decisions were 100% original, and AI only made the execution faster.
